0.title: Zephaniah: He Will Rejoice Over You
0.overview:
The message. Zephaniah begins with God sweeping the earth bare and ends with God singing. In between he speaks to a people who had grown comfortable with God. The day of the LORD is near: a day when God will judge sin in the open, beginning with his own people, and when “Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them” (1:18). Yet there is a way through that day: “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land” (2:3). Those who take refuge in him will find that the God they feared is the God who “will rejoice over you with gladness” (3:17).

Background: the prophet. All we know of Zephaniah comes from his first verse. He traces his family back four generations, further than any other prophet, to Hezekiah (1:1). Most take this to be King Hezekiah, which would make Zephaniah a distant relative of the king he preached under; the verse does not say so, but no other reason for so long a family tree is obvious. If so, he had access to the court, and used it to say hard things about “the officials and the king’s sons” (1:8). His name probably means “the LORD hides”, fitting for the prophet who tells the humble that they “may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD” (2:3).

When and where. He preached “in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah” (1:1), who reigned from about 640 to 609 BC. Josiah came to the throne as a boy of eight, after the long reign of his grandfather Manasseh, who had put altars to the stars in the temple courts and “shed very much innocent blood” (2 Kings 21:16). Zephaniah’s Jerusalem is still Manasseh’s Jerusalem: Baal worship, star worship on the flat roofs (1:5), and the LORD sworn by alongside Milcom, the god of Ammon. So he most likely spoke before Josiah’s great reform, perhaps about 630 BC, and his preaching may have helped to prepare it. About 622 BC the Book of the Law was found in the temple, and Josiah removed the very priests Zephaniah names (2 Kings 22:8; 23:5). Jeremiah was called in the same reign (Jeremiah 1:2). Some date Zephaniah a little later, reading “the remnant of Baal” (1:4) as a sign that the purge had begun; nothing in the message depends on it.

The world of the book. For a century Assyria had ruled the Near East from Nineveh. It had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and made Judah a subject state, but by Josiah’s day it was weakening. Zephaniah foresaw its capital, the city that said “I am, and there is no one else” (2:15), become a desert where owls nest; Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. But the power that replaced Assyria brought Judah’s own day of the LORD. Josiah was killed at Megiddo in 609 BC, his sons undid his work, and in 586 BC Nebuchadnezzar burned Jerusalem and its temple. The reform had not reached the nation’s heart: “Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath” (2 Kings 23:26).

The kind of writing. Zephaniah is prophecy in Hebrew poetry, loud and vivid: God searching Jerusalem with lamps (1:12), a sacrifice with Judah on the altar (1:7), something hooting from the windows of empty Nineveh (2:14). From the Latin of 1:15 comes Dies Irae, “day of wrath”, the medieval hymn the church sang for centuries. Like other prophets, Zephaniah sees near and far together, so the coming fall of Jerusalem and the last judgment of the whole earth are spoken of in the same breath.

How the book makes its case. Chapter 1 announces “The great day of the LORD” (1:14). It opens by undoing creation, man, beast, birds and fish swept away in the reverse of Genesis 1 (1:2–3), then turns on Judah (1:4–13). Three kinds of people are named: open idolaters; hedgers who “swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom” (1:5); and drifters “who do not seek the LORD or inquire of him” (1:6). God will search the city for the complacent, who say, “The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill” (1:12). Chapter 2 opens a door: “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land” (2:3). Then judgment sweeps round the compass, from the Philistine coast to Moab and Ammon, Cush and Assyria (2:4–15): no nation is beyond God’s reach. Chapter 3 turns back to Jerusalem, whose officials, judges, prophets and priests have all failed, though “The LORD within her is righteous” (3:1–7). Then God says, “wait for me” (3:8), and everything changes. He will purify the speech of the peoples, undoing Babel, “that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD” (3:9), leave “a people humble and lowly” who take refuge in him (3:12), and tell Zion to sing, because the King is in her midst (3:14–20). The book moves from fire to song, and the hinge is 2:3.

Past or still to come? Some read Zephaniah only as history, fulfilled when Babylon came, and take its worldwide language (1:2–3, 18) as poetic overstatement; others read it only as a forecast of the end of the world. Many critical scholars also think the bright promises of 3:9–20 were added after the exile. This commentary’s view is that the book is one message from one prophet, and that its day is both: it fell on Jerusalem in 586 BC, and that fall was an advance picture of the last day, which the New Testament calls “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:8).

Where it leads: to Christ. The New Testament never quotes Zephaniah by name, but it echoes him, and the book leads to Christ by the need it exposes and the promise it makes. The need is in one word of 2:3: “perhaps you may be hidden.” Zephaniah could not say how sinners might be sheltered. The gospel can. When Jesus hung on the cross, “there was darkness over the whole land” (Mark 15:33): the darkness of the day of wrath (1:15) fell on one man in his people’s place. Silver and gold deliver no one (1:18), but believers were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). So “perhaps” becomes certainty: our “life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). The promise is in 3:15: “The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst.” It came true in Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), greeted in Jerusalem with words that seem to join Zechariah 9:9 to Zephaniah’s “Fear not, O Zion” (3:16): “Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming” (John 12:15). And the God who sings over his people is the God whose Son “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). The joy was his people.

For us. Zephaniah asks which of the three people in chapter 1 we are: the one with an open rival to God; the one who keeps another god in reserve, money or reputation, in case God fails; or the one who has simply stopped seeking him. It names the commonest unbelief inside churches, the shrug of 1:12, a God who will never actually do anything. And it gives all three the same answer: seek the LORD, humbly, now. Many Christians can believe that God puts up with them, or even forgives them. Zephaniah says more. In Christ the God who searched Jerusalem with lamps is glad about his people, quiets them by his love as a parent quiets a frightened child, and sings over them (3:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s judgment begins at home, and it falls on divided and drifting worship as surely as on open idolatry. Zephaniah introduces himself with an unusually long family tree and dates his preaching to the reign of Josiah (v. 1). Then God speaks at full volume: he will sweep away man and beast, birds and fish, undoing creation in reverse (vv. 2–3). The hand stretched over the whole earth comes down first on Judah and Jerusalem (v. 4), and on three kinds of people: those who worship the stars from their roofs, those who swear by the LORD and by Milcom too, and those who have simply stopped seeking him (vv. 5–6). None of them has left the temple; all of them have left God.
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgment begins with his own people, and includes those who add other gods to him as well as those who quietly drift away.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah the son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah. "I will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth," declares the LORD. "I will sweep away man and beast; I will sweep away the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, and the rubble with the wicked. I will cut off mankind from the face of the earth," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens the book by announcing that he will undo the world he made, because sin has spoiled it to the root.

Son of Hezekiah. Zephaniah traces his family back four generations, further than any other prophet. The likeliest reason is that this is King Hezekiah, which would make Zephaniah a distant relative of the king he preached under (see the introduction). He used his access to say hard things (v. 8).

In the days of Josiah. Josiah later purged the land of idols (2 Kings 23:4–14). The idolatry described here was still in full operation, so Zephaniah probably preached before those reforms and may have helped to bring them about.

I will utterly sweep away everything. The book opens at full volume. Listen to the order of the creatures: man and beast, the birds of the heavens, the fish of the sea. Genesis names them the other way round, fish, birds, beasts, man (Genesis 1:26). Creation is being undone. Sin does more than break rules; it unravels the world God made, and his judgment lets that unravelling run to its end. Even the idols go onto the rubbish heap with those who served them (see the box below).

Truth before comfort. This book ends with God singing over his people (3:17), but it begins here. The Bible’s comfort is never cheap: it is spoken to people who have first been told the truth about their sin. And the God who threatens to undo his creation will, through his Son, remake it (Revelation 21:5).

Will God really sweep away everything, despite his promise after the flood? The words describe how far the day of the LORD reaches: it fell first on Judah in 586 BC, and it will be complete at the last judgment. God promised Noah never again to destroy the earth by flood (Genesis 9:11); the final judgment is by fire, and it leads not to emptiness but to a new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13).

Uncertain wording. “The rubble with the wicked” is a difficult phrase. The ESV notes that “rubble” may mean “stumbling blocks”, most likely idols, the things that tripped the people into sin. The sense, that the wicked and what led them astray go together, is clear; the exact word is not.
verseByVerse.note: Josiah reigned about 640–609 BC; the Book of the Law was found in the temple in his eighteenth year (2 Kgs 22:3-8).

verseByVerse.quote: "I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off from this place the remnant of Baal and the name of the idolatrous priests along with the priests, those who bow down on the roofs to the host of the heavens, those who bow down and swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom, those who have turned back from following the LORD, who do not seek the LORD or inquire of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment starts with God’s own people, and it falls not only on open idolaters but on those who divide their loyalty and those who have quietly stopped seeking him.

I will stretch out my hand against Judah. The hand that reached over the whole earth comes down first on his own people (compare 1 Peter 4:17). “The remnant of Baal” suggests that Baal worship had already been cut back, and God means to finish the job. Half-cleared idolatry is still idolatry.

The idolatrous priests along with the priests. Pagan priests and the LORD’s own priests together: when God judges a nation, he starts with its religion. Then come three kinds of people, and most of us are somewhere in the list.

Those who bow down on the roofs. First, the frank pagans, who went up on the flat roofs at night to worship “the host of the heavens”, the sun, moon and stars (see the introduction). Josiah later removed exactly these priests (2 Kings 23:5).

And yet swear by Milcom. Second, and more subtly, those who “bow down and swear to the LORD and yet swear by Milcom”, the god of Ammon. They have not left the faith; they have added to it, keeping another god in reserve in case the LORD fails them. Today the second god is rarely a statue; it is money, a career or someone’s approval, whatever we would turn to if God let us down.

Who do not seek the LORD. Third, the drifters. No other god is mentioned at all. They simply stopped: they “have turned back from following the LORD” and do “not seek the LORD or inquire of him”. No dramatic apostasy, no decision to walk away; prayer thinned out, then stopped. God names this alongside star worship, which should trouble anyone whose faith has quietly gone cold.

A door left open. The trouble is meant to wake, not to crush. The next chapter opens a door to people like this: “Seek the LORD” (2:3). One Israelite never turned back: when the road led to a cross, Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), and his faithfulness is counted to every drifter who comes home to him. A believer who grieves that his prayers have thinned is not one of the complacent of verse 12; the grief itself is a sign that God is stirring him.

Uncertain wording. Where the ESV has “Milcom”, its note says the Hebrew may be read “their king”. The letters allow either, and either way the point stands: a rival lord sworn by alongside the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: Josiah later defiled the high place Solomon had built for Milcom east of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Sacrifice and a Search
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the LORD is a sacrifice, and God will search every corner of his city for those who think he does nothing. A hush falls before the Lord GOD, because the sacrifice is ready and the victim is Judah (v. 7). God names the governing class, those who dress like the nations, the superstitious and the dishonest (vv. 8–9), then walks his hearers through their own city as it falls, from the Fish Gate to the silent market (vv. 10–11). Last of all he lights a lamp to find the complacent, who say he will do neither good nor ill, and lets the curses of the covenant take their houses and vineyards (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing escapes God's search, least of all the comfortable unbelief that assumes he does nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Be silent before the Lord GOD! For the day of the LORD is near; the LORD has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests. And on the day of the LORD's sacrifice— "I will punish the officials and the king's sons and all who array themselves in foreign attire. On that day I will punish everyone who leaps over the threshold, and those who fill their master's house with violence and fraud. "On that day," declares the LORD, "a cry will be heard from the Fish Gate, a wail from the Second Quarter, a loud crash from the hills. Wail, O inhabitants of the Mortar! For all the traders are no more; all who weigh out silver are cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD is coming like a sacrifice with Judah on the altar, and it will reach every class and corner of the city, from the palace to the market.

Be silent before the Lord GOD! Habakkuk, preaching around the same time, ended his second chapter with the same hush (Habakkuk 2:20). There comes a point when the arguing stops and everyone falls silent before the Judge.

The LORD has prepared a sacrifice. In Israel a sacrifice was usually followed by a feast. But who is on the table? Judah itself. The guests God has “consecrated”, set apart for the meal, are the invading armies he will summon. Revelation uses the same terrible picture of the last battle, where birds are called to “the great supper of God” (Revelation 19:17).

The officials and the king’s sons. God names names: the governing class, Zephaniah’s own relatives. “Foreign attire” is not about fashion; dressing like the surrounding nations was a public statement about whose culture, and whose gods, you admired.

Everyone who leaps over the threshold. Probably a pagan superstition: the priests of Dagon in Philistia would not tread on the threshold of his temple (1 Samuel 5:5). Then the plain charge: those “who fill their master’s house with violence and fraud”. Superstition and dishonesty travel together, because both are attempts to control life without God.

A cry will be heard from the Fish Gate. Zephaniah walks his hearers through their own city as it falls: the Fish Gate in the north wall; the Second Quarter, a newer district where the prophetess Huldah lived (2 Kings 22:14); and “the Mortar”, probably a hollow where the market stood. The sound rises from a cry to a wail to a crash.

All the traders are no more. Then the business district falls silent: “all who weigh out silver” on their scales “are cut off”. Judgment reaches the shops and the counting tables, not only the temples.

Another sacrifice, another silence. In Zephaniah the LORD prepares a sacrifice, and his people are on the altar. At Calvary God prepared a sacrifice again, and his own Son was on it, so that those who trust him need never be. Every mouth is stopped before God’s law (Romans 3:19), but someone else was silent before a judge for us: “like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Because Christ stood speechless in our place, the hush of judgment becomes for his people a different quiet, the one Zephaniah promises at the end of his book: “he will quiet you by his love” (3:17).

What this silence looks like. Stop the defence. When conscience accuses you, do not explain, compare and excuse; name the sin plainly. Make room to listen. Before you pray through your list, sit for a few minutes with an open Bible and let him speak first: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Do not put him on trial. When his providence baffles you, you may lament honestly, but you need not demand that he explain himself.

Uncertain wording. “Leaps over the threshold” is probably a superstition, though some take it of bursting into houses to rob them. For “their master’s house” the ESV notes “their Lord’s”, which would point to the temple; “traders” may be “the people of Canaan”, an old name that came to mean merchants; and where “the Mortar” lay is unknown. The overall picture is clear.
verseByVerse.note: The Fish Gate probably took its name from the fish brought to market there (compare Neh 13:16).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are complacent, those who say in their hearts, 'The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill.' Their goods shall be plundered, and their houses laid waste. Though they build houses, they shall not inhabit them; though they plant vineyards, they shall not drink wine from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will search out the comfortable who assume he will never act, and the life they built without him will be taken from them.

I will search Jerusalem with lamps. God comes through the city with lamps, like a man searching a dark cellar, bending into every corner. Nobody is overlooked because they are unimportant, and nobody escapes because they are respectable: “no creature is hidden from his sight” (Hebrews 4:13).

The men who are complacent. He is looking first not for the murderers but for the complacent. The ESV notes that the Hebrew pictures wine left undisturbed until it thickens on its dregs: settled, unstirred, going thick (compare Jeremiah 48:11).

The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill. Their creed is not atheism. They believe God exists; they simply assume he will never actually step in, to bless or to judge, so life can be arranged without reference to him. It is probably the commonest form of unbelief inside churches, and God takes a lamp and goes looking for exactly those people.

The God who never interferes. The creed has a long history. Epicurus, the Greek philosopher, taught that the gods exist but live in untroubled bliss far away and never meddle in human affairs, and he offered this as good news: there is nothing to fear. Many now hold something close to it: God is in the background, kindly and unbothered; he will not judge us, and he will not ask much of us. It feels like freedom. But read the creed again. A God who never acts against you never acts for you either. If he will not judge the oppressor, he will not rescue the oppressed; if he will not trouble your conscience, he will not answer your prayer. The comfortable men of Jerusalem bought a quiet life with a useless God.

The God who came. The gospel is the opposite. God did interfere, decisively: he came down into the middle of our history in his Son, took the judgment on himself, and rose to do his people good for ever.

Though they build houses, they shall not inhabit them. Verse 13 is one of the curses God’s covenant had warned of for disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:30): houses built and never lived in, vineyards planted and never tasted. Jesus told of a rich man who planned to say to his soul, “relax, eat, drink, be merry”, and heard God say, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:19–20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day is near, terrible and beyond the reach of money, and it comes because people have sinned against the LORD. The pace quickens, “near, near and hastening fast”, and even the soldier cries out (v. 14). Then the word “day” falls like a hammer six times over: wrath, distress, ruin, darkness, clouds, trumpet (vv. 15–16). The reason is stated plainly, and the cost is everything people held precious (v. 17). Silver and gold, which buy a way out of most troubles, buy nothing here, and the fire of God’s jealousy reaches the whole earth (v. 18). The chapter leaves its hearers asking where anyone could hide, and the next chapter answers.
verseByVerse.theology: The day of the LORD is certain, near and beyond the reach of money.

verseByVerse.quote: The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast; the sound of the day of the LORD is bitter; the mighty man cries aloud there. A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness, a day of trumpet blast and battle cry against the fortified cities and against the lofty battlements. I will bring distress on mankind, so that they shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the LORD; their blood shall be poured out like dust, and their flesh like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD. In the fire of his jealousy, all the earth shall be consumed; for a full and sudden end he will make of all the inhabitants of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD is near and certain, a day of wrath on sin that no one can buy their way out of; only a shelter God himself provides will stand.

The great day of the LORD is near. The drumbeat begins: “near, near and hastening fast”. And the one crying out is “the mighty man”, the professional soldier, the one who is supposed to stay steady when everyone else panics.

A day of wrath is that day. Six times in two verses: “a day”. The repetition is the point; the hammer falls again and again. From the Latin of verse 15 comes the medieval hymn Dies Irae, “day of wrath”, which the church sang for centuries.

What is the day of the LORD? In the prophets it is any day when God steps in openly to judge and to save, and each such day points to the last one (Joel 2:1–2; Amos 5:18–20). These verses describe the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and the last day, of which that fall was an advance picture. The New Testament calls it “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:8), for God will judge the world by the man he has appointed (Acts 17:31).

They shall walk like the blind. People will grope about with no idea where to go, and the reason is stated without decoration: “because they have sinned against the LORD”. Their blood and flesh, so precious to them, will be treated as dust and dung.

Neither their silver nor their gold. The last verse removes the final hope of the men at the scales (v. 11). Money can buy an escape from most things; it buys nothing here. Proverbs says the same: “Riches do not profit in the day of wrath” (Proverbs 11:4). “The fire of his jealousy” is not petty envy but the burning loyalty of a husband whose wife has given herself to others. A God who did not mind would not love.

Not with silver or gold. The judge on that day is the one who was judged in his people’s place. When he hung on the cross, “there was darkness over the whole land” (Mark 15:33): the darkness of verse 15 fell on one man. So Peter tells Christians they were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). There is exactly one shelter from that day: “Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come” (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should live in dread of that day: for those in Christ it is the day of rescue, and God tells the faithful to “wait for me” (3:8; Romans 8:1). But no one may presume on it while living as they please: “Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD!” (Amos 5:18).
verseByVerse.note: The hymn is traditionally credited to Thomas of Celano, a thirteenth-century Franciscan.

1.title: The Great Day of the LORD
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the book with a family tree and a date, “in the days of Josiah”, probably before that king’s great reform (see the introduction). Then God speaks of undoing the world he made, and brings that word home to Jerusalem.

The message. The day of the LORD is near, and it begins with God’s own people. God is not the absent, harmless deity the comfortable imagine: he sees the idolater, the one who hedges his bets and the one who has stopped praying, and on that day nothing people lean on will hold, not religion, rank or money: “Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them” (v. 18).

Why it was said. Jerusalem still bore the marks of Manasseh’s long reign: Baal worship, star worship on the roofs, the LORD sworn by alongside Milcom (see the introduction). Worse was the settled assumption among the prosperous that God would never actually do anything (v. 12). A people that comfortable had to hear the thunder before they could hear the invitation of 2:3.

How the chapter makes its case. Zephaniah begins as wide as possible, with creation run backwards (vv. 1–3). Then the circle tightens on Judah and its three kinds of unfaithful worshipper (vv. 4–6). A hush falls, for God has prepared a sacrifice and Judah is on the altar; the officials, the superstitious and the dishonest are named, and a cry crosses the city from the Fish Gate to the market (vv. 7–11). God lights a lamp and searches for the complacent, whose houses and vineyards will go to others (vv. 12–13). Finally the word “day” falls like a hammer, wrath, darkness, trumpet and blood, with a fire no silver can buy off (vv. 14–18).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes, and by pattern. It describes a day no one can survive on their own resources, and as yet offers no shelter. The New Testament shows where it is. When Christ died “there was darkness over the whole land” (Mark 15:33): the darkness of the day of wrath (v. 15) fell on the one man who had not sinned, and his blood, not silver or gold, ransomed his people (1 Peter 1:18–19). Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC was a preview of the last day, “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:8).

For us. Ask which of the three people of verses 4–6 you most resemble, and do not assume the answer is none. The shrug of verse 12 is the commonest unbelief in comfortable churches, and its cure is not more religion but taking God seriously again. The chapter’s terror is meant to drive us to the one shelter that holds on that day: the Christ who bore its wrath.
1.theology:
Sin unravels the world God made, and his judgment lets that unravelling run its course (vv. 2-3; Gen 1:26).

Judgment begins with God's own people and with their religion (vv. 4-5; 1 Pet 4:17).

Dividing our trust between God and a second god is as serious as open paganism, and quiet drift is named alongside both (vv. 5-6).

There is a point where argument ends and silence before God is the only response (v. 7; Hab 2:20).

God searches out the comfortable unbelief that assumes he will never act (v. 12).

The day of the LORD is near, certain and terrible, and the fall of Jerusalem was an advance picture of it (vv. 14-16).

Wealth cannot buy deliverance on that day; only the ransom God provides can (v. 18; Prov 11:4; 1 Pet 1:18).
1.examples:
Zephaniah lists the creatures of Genesis 1 in reverse, as if creation were being undone, and throws the idols out with the people who served them. He sees worshippers who swear by God and keep a second god in reserve, and others who never walked out but whose praying simply thinned and stopped.

His pictures of the day are unforgettable: a sacrifice where the guests are invading armies, God going through the city with a lamp and looking into the corners, wine left so long undisturbed that it thickens on its dregs, and silver and gold that buy nothing at all on that one day.

keyVerse.quote: The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast; the sound of the day of the LORD is bitter; the mighty man cries aloud there.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s alarm bell, and it gives the whole book its theme. The day Judah assumed would never come is near and coming fast, and even the strong will cry out. The New Testament calls it the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, so the only safe place to hear this verse is in him, who bore its wrath for his people.

1.reflection:
Verses 4–6 describe three kinds of unfaithful worshipper: the open idolater, the one who swears by the LORD and by Milcom, and the one who has simply stopped seeking him. Which is the greatest danger in our churches today, and which in your own life? What might a “second god kept in reserve” look like for you?

The complacent of verse 12 believe God exists but assume he will never do anything. Why is that belief so comfortable, and what does it cost? How would your week look different if you truly expected God to act, both for you and against sin?

Verse 18 says silver and gold cannot deliver on the day of wrath, and 1 Peter 1:18–19 says we were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the blood of Christ. What do people around you trust to keep them safe? How does the cross change the way a Christian hears the warnings of this chapter?

Zephaniah begins with judgment and ends with God singing over his people (3:17). Why do you think the Bible insists on telling us the truth about sin before it comforts us? What is lost when churches skip the first part?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Perhaps You May Be Hidden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the day of the LORD arrives there is still time, and the only safe course is to seek the LORD himself in humility. Zephaniah calls the shameless nation to gather, and the word “before” sounds four times: before the decree takes effect, before the day blows away like chaff, before the burning anger comes (vv. 1–2). Then comes the hinge of the whole book, spoken to the humble who still do what God says: seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility (v. 3). He promises no automatic escape, only “perhaps you may be hidden”, but that careful word opens a door which the rest of Scripture flings wide.
verseByVerse.theology: The only shelter from the day of wrath is God himself, and the door stands open to the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: Gather together, yes, gather, O shameless nation, before the decree takes effect —before the day passes away like chaff— before there comes upon you the burning anger of the LORD, before there comes upon you the day of the anger of the LORD. Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the day of God’s anger arrives there is still time, and the one way through it is to seek the LORD himself, humbly and at once.

Gather together, yes, gather. After the thunder of chapter 1 comes an urgent appeal: bring the people before God. The word “before” beats four times. There is still time, and it is running out; the day will blow past like chaff from a threshing floor.

O shameless nation. That is the problem exactly: a nation that can still feel shame is not far from turning back.

Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land. The call goes not to the officials or the wealthy of chapter 1 but to ordinary people who still did what God said, the kind God has never been short of, though they are usually unnoticed. Three times: seek. Seek the LORD: not an experience, not safety, but God himself. Seek righteousness: the just dealing chapter 1 found missing in the market. Seek humility, impossible to boast of having found; it is the humble who are told to seek it, because those who have most know they need more. None of this earns shelter: it is turning toward the God who is already calling, and it is his Spirit who stirs the seeking.

Perhaps you may be hidden. Not “you will certainly escape”. Zephaniah will not turn God’s mercy into a mechanism. Other prophets speak the same way: “Who knows whether he will not turn and relent” (Joel 2:14; compare Amos 5:15; Jonah 3:9). This is not doubt about God’s kindness; it is a refusal to presume on it.

A hiding place. There is a hiding place on the day of wrath (Psalm 27:5), and it is a person. Zephaniah’s “perhaps” becomes certainty at the cross, where the anger of that day fell on Christ, so that the believer’s “life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). And behind all our seeking stands a greater one: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). We seek him because we were first sought.

How do I seek the LORD? Seeking is not a mood but ordinary habits that turn your face toward him. Go where he speaks. Open his word each day, even for ten minutes before the phone, and ask what it shows you of him. Tell him you want him. Pray plainly, taking him at his promise: “You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). Seek righteousness where you work. Make one dealing this week honest even if it costs you. Seek humility on purpose. Ask someone who knows you where you are hard to correct, and listen without defending yourself: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6). Keep company with the humble. Gather with ordinary believers on the Lord’s Day; seeking is rarely done alone.

Uncertain wording. Verses 1–2 are among the hardest lines in the book. “Gather” is a verb normally used of gathering stubble, and “shameless” may instead mean “without longing” or “undesired”. For “takes effect” the ESV notes the Hebrew “gives birth”: the decree is like a pregnancy moving to its day. In verse 3 “who do his just commands” may be “who carry out his judgment”. The thrust is clear: seek the LORD before it is too late.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No neighbour of God’s people is beyond his reach, and his judgments clear the ground for a remnant and for the worship of the nations. Judgment sweeps west first, to the Philistine coast: its great cities will be emptied, and the land will become pasture where Judah’s remnant lies down safely (vv. 4–7). Then east, to Moab and Ammon, kin of Israel who mocked her: God has heard every taunt, and their pride will leave them like Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 8–10). The section ends with the horizon opening: God will starve the gods of the earth, and every land of the nations will bow to him, each in its own place (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God judges the mockers of his people and then gathers the nations he has humbled.

verseByVerse.quote: For Gaza shall be deserted, and Ashkelon shall become a desolation; Ashdod's people shall be driven out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to you inhabitants of the seacoast, you nation of the Cherethites! The word of the LORD is against you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines; and I will destroy you until no inhabitant is left. And you, O seacoast, shall be pastures, with meadows for shepherds and folds for flocks. The seacoast shall become the possession of the remnant of the house of Judah, on which they shall graze, and in the houses of Ashkelon they shall lie down at evening. For the LORD their God will be mindful of them and restore their fortunes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment reaches Judah’s oldest enemies on the coast, and clears their land to become a safe pasture for his remnant.

Round the compass. Zephaniah now turns to the nations, west, east, south and north, starting with the Philistines, Israel’s oldest enemies. “Driven out at noon” suggests an attack so confident that it comes in broad daylight, when armies usually rested from the heat.

Gaza shall be deserted. The line is built from puns English cannot keep. Gaza (ʿAzzah) will be deserted (ʿazubah), and Ekron (ʿEqron) uprooted (teʿaqer). Each city hears its sentence in the sound of its own name.

You nation of the Cherethites! The name probably recalls the Philistines’ origins in Crete (compare Amos 9:7), and calling their land “Canaan” sets them among the peoples whose land God had promised to Israel.

Pastures, with meadows for shepherds. The busy coastal plain, crowded with fortified cities and trade, will become quiet grazing land with folds for flocks. Sheep will crop grass where the markets were.

The remnant of the house of Judah. Here, quietly, is the first promise of the book: God will have a people left, lying down safely in the very houses of their old enemies. “The LORD their God will be mindful of them and restore their fortunes”: he has not forgotten them, even when the news is all judgment.

Did Judah possess the Philistine coast? Jews did settle parts of it in the second century BC under the Maccabees, the Jewish family who won independence from the Greek kings. But the promise reaches further: the remnant who graze safely are the flock of the Good Shepherd, who promised, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5; see the note on 3:18–20).

Uncertain wording. The word rendered “meadows” is rare; the ESV notes that it may mean “caves”, perhaps shepherds’ shelters, and it may be a play on “Cherethites” in verse 5. Either way, the picture is of flocks where cities stood.
verseByVerse.note: Gath, the fifth Philistine city, is missing here, as it is in Amos 1:6-8 and Jeremiah 25:20; it may already have lost its importance.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have heard the taunts of Moab and the revilings of the Ammonites, how they have taunted my people and made boasts against their territory. Therefore, as I live," declares the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, "Moab shall become like Sodom, and the Ammonites like Gomorrah, a land possessed by nettles and salt pits, and a waste forever. The remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the survivors of my nation shall possess them." This shall be their lot in return for their pride, because they taunted and boasted against the people of the LORD of hosts. The LORD will be awesome against them; for he will famish all the gods of the earth, and to him shall bow down, each in its place, all the lands of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears every taunt against his people and brings the proud mockers down, and in the end he starves every false god until all the nations bow to him.

I have heard the taunts of Moab. East of the Jordan lay Moab and Ammon, descended from Lot (Genesis 19:36–38), related to Israel and endlessly hostile. Their sin here is not invasion but mockery: taunts, revilings, boasts against Judah’s land. And God says, “I have heard”. Words spoken against God’s people are heard in heaven, a comfort to anyone sneered at for their faith.

Moab shall become like Sodom. Moab lay along the Dead Sea, near where Sodom and Gomorrah had been overthrown (Genesis 19), the cities their ancestor Lot had fled. Their own neighbourhood was the warning they ignored. Now nettles and salt pits, the growth of ruined ground, will take their fields.

In return for their pride. The verdict names the root. Mockery is pride with a voice. Other prophets said the same of Moab: “We have heard of the pride of Moab” (Isaiah 16:6; Jeremiah 48:29).

He will famish all the gods of the earth. God will starve the gods of the sacrifices that kept their temples running. Then the horizon opens: “to him shall bow down, each in its place, all the lands of the nations”. The phrase “each in its place” matters. The nations will not need to travel to Jerusalem; worship will reach them where they live. Jesus told the woman at the well that the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem, but “in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–23).

The promise to Abraham. Here the old promise surfaces, that in Abraham “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). Every church planted among a people who once served other gods is verse 11 coming true, and one day “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may cheer at the ruin of those who mock them. Because God has heard, his people need not answer taunt with taunt: “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them” (Romans 12:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest powers on earth fall as surely as the furthest, and self-sufficiency ends in ruin. One line dispatches Cush in the far south (v. 12). Then God turns north to Assyria and its capital Nineveh, which ruled the known world: it will become a dry waste where flocks and wild creatures lodge, birds call from the empty windows, and the costly cedar panelling lies open to the weather (vv. 13–14). Its epitaph quotes its own boast, “I am, and there is no one else”, words that belong to God alone, and it ends as a sight people hiss at (v. 15). The humble of verse 3 say instead, “He is”.
verseByVerse.theology: A city that claims God's own "I am" for itself ends as a ruin where wild birds nest.

verseByVerse.quote: You also, O Cushites, shall be slain by my sword. And he will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria, and he will make Nineveh a desolation, a dry waste like the desert. Herds shall lie down in her midst, all kinds of beasts; even the owl and the hedgehog shall lodge in her capitals; a voice shall hoot in the window; devastation will be on the threshold; for her cedar work will be laid bare. This is the exultant city that lived securely, that said in her heart, "I am, and there is no one else." What a desolation she has become, a lair for wild beasts! Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither distance nor power is any protection: the far south and the mighty north fall alike, and the proud city that claimed God’s place becomes a ruin.

You also, O Cushites. South now, to Cush, the region beyond Egypt (see the note on 3:10). One short line for a distant people: distance is no protection. Kings from Cush had ruled Egypt itself for much of the previous century, so the line probably takes in the whole southern power.

He will make Nineveh a desolation. Then north to the superpower itself, whose armies came on Israel from the north. Nineveh, capital of the known world, will become “a dry waste like the desert”. Nahum preached the same message at length; here it takes three verses. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, within a generation of these words.

Even the owl and the hedgehog. Herds sleep in the streets, wild creatures lodge on the carved capitals of the palace columns, and something hoots from an empty window frame. The costly cedar panelling, brought from Lebanon at great expense, lies open to the weather.

I am, and there is no one else. Here is the city’s epitaph, and its boast is blasphemy. It is almost word for word what God says of himself: “I am the LORD, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:5). Babylon would later say the same, “I am, and there is no one besides me”, and fall because of it (Isaiah 47:8; compare Revelation 18:7). That is what self-sufficiency finally claims, whether a superpower says it or a heart says it quietly: there is no one else who matters, and I answer to nobody. The chapter ends with passers-by hissing at the ruin.

Why verse 3 stands here. Between the judgment of Judah and the judgment of the nations, God put an open door: “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land”. The proud city said “I am”; the humble say “He is”, and are hidden. The only one who could rightly say “I am” did not count equality with God “a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7). Nineveh grasped at God’s name and was brought to dust; the Son who humbled himself was given “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the creatures rendered “owl” and “hedgehog” cannot be identified with certainty, and that “all kinds of beasts” is literally “beasts of every nation”. “A voice shall hoot in the window” is literally “a voice shall sing”. The picture of a great city given over to wild creatures is clear.

2.title: Seek the LORD, All You Humble
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with the whole earth consumed in the fire of God’s jealousy. Chapter 2 opens with the hinge of the book: before the day arrives, a door is opened (vv. 1–3). Then the judgment that began with Judah sweeps outward over the nations around her.

The message. There is still time, and there is one way through the coming day: seek the LORD, humbly, now. No nation is beyond God’s reach, and none of the powers that mocked or terrified his people will stand. But the God who brings down the proud will keep a remnant, give them what their enemies held, and bring the nations to bow before him.

Why it was said. Judah lived among old enemies, the Philistines to the west and Moab and Ammon across the Jordan, under the shadow of Assyria to the north (see the introduction). Some of Zephaniah’s hearers were shameless; others were humble and frightened, wondering whether anyone would survive. To the first he says, gather and seek; to the second he shows that the nations they feared are in God’s hand.

How the chapter makes its case. The shameless nation is told to gather before the decree takes effect, and the humble to seek the LORD, righteousness and humility, that “perhaps” they may be hidden (vv. 1–3). Then judgment goes round the compass. West: the Philistine cities will be emptied, and their coast become pasture for Judah’s remnant (vv. 4–7). East: Moab and Ammon, who taunted God’s people, will become like Sodom and Gomorrah, while God starves the gods of the earth and the nations bow to him (vv. 8–11). South: Cush falls by his sword (v. 12). North: Nineveh, the city that said “I am, and there is no one else”, becomes a ruin where owls nest and passers-by hiss (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and the promise it holds out. Zephaniah’s “perhaps you may be hidden” is honest: he could not say how sinners might be sheltered on the day of God’s anger. The gospel answers him, because that anger fell on Christ, and the believer’s “life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). The promise of verse 11, that every land will bow to the LORD each in its place, is the promise to Abraham coming into view, kept as the gospel goes to the nations, until every knee bows at the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:10).

For us. The call of verse 3 is for everyone who reads this chapter: seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility. Nineveh’s boast can be whispered by a heart as easily as shouted by an empire, and it ends the same way. The humble have a hiding place, and it is a person.
2.theology:
There is a "before" in God's dealings: warnings are given while there is still time to turn (vv. 1-2).

Seeking God himself, with righteousness and humility, is the only shelter on the day of wrath (v. 3; Ps 27:5).

God's mercy may be sought but never presumed upon: "perhaps you may be hidden" (v. 3; Joel 2:14; Amos 5:15; Jonah 3:9).

God hears what is said against his people, and mockery is pride with a voice (vv. 8, 10).

God starves the idols of the nations and gathers worshippers from every land, each where they are (v. 11; John 4:23).

Distance and power are no protection from God (vv. 12-13).

Self-sufficiency finally claims God's own name for itself, and ends in ruin (v. 15; Isa 45:5; 47:8).
2.examples:
The chapter opens with four urgent "befores" in one sentence and a promise that says "perhaps" and means it, spoken to the invisible community of humble people God has never been without.

Then the pictures of judgment: sheep grazing where the Philistine markets used to be, taunts against God's people heard in heaven, gods starved of sacrifices until they fade away, and an owl nesting on the carved top of a palace column in a city whose last word was "I am".

keyVerse.quote: Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the book, standing between the judgment of Judah and the judgment of the nations. It gives the only safe response to the coming day: not self-defence but seeking God himself, with righteousness and humility. Its honest “perhaps” is answered in the gospel, where those who seek the LORD are hidden with Christ in God.

2.reflection:
Verse 3 tells people who are already humble to seek humility. Why might the humble be the ones who know they need more of it? What would it look like for you to seek the LORD, righteousness and humility this week?

Zephaniah says only “perhaps you may be hidden”. How does the gospel turn that “perhaps” into certainty (Colossians 3:3)? Why is the prophet’s caution still a healthy check on presuming on God’s mercy?

God says of Moab and Ammon, “I have heard the taunts” (v. 8). How does knowing that God hears every sneer against his people help you respond to mockery without bitterness or retaliation?

Nineveh said, “I am, and there is no one else” (v. 15). In what quieter ways do people, churches and nations make the same claim today? Where do you hear it in your own heart?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s own city is as guilty as the nations, yet the righteous LORD has not left her, and the faithful are told to wait for him. The woe that fell on Nineveh now falls on Jerusalem: rebellious, defiled, deaf to every voice and far from her God (vv. 1–2). Her officials prey like lions and her judges like wolves, her prophets are faithless and her priests twist the law (vv. 3–4). In the middle of it all the LORD does justice every morning, but the unjust feel no shame (v. 5). God cut off other nations so that his people would learn, and they grew worse (vv. 6–7). So he says, “wait for me”, for the day he gathers the nations to judgment (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's steady daily justice stands in the middle of a corrupt city, and the call to his people is to wait for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled, the oppressing city! She listens to no voice; she accepts no correction. She does not trust in the LORD; she does not draw near to her God. Her officials within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves that leave nothing till the morning. Her prophets are fickle, treacherous men; her priests profane what is holy; they do violence to the law. The LORD within her is righteous; he does no injustice; every morning he shows forth his justice; each dawn he does not fail; but the unjust knows no shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem, the city God chose, has become as corrupt as the nations around her, yet the LORD has not left her: he is in her midst, doing right every morning.

The oppressing city. After Nineveh we expect another foreign capital, but the oppressing city is Jerusalem. God’s own city hears the kind of woe Nahum pronounced over Nineveh (Nahum 3:1).

She listens to no voice. Verse 2 lists four failures that read like a diagnosis of spiritual decline in any life. She listens to no voice: God has spoken and she will not hear. She accepts no correction: rebuke bounces off. She does not trust in the LORD: she relies on politics and money instead. She does not draw near to her God: prayer has stopped. Deafness, defensiveness, distrust, distance.

Her officials within her are roaring lions. Four groups of leaders, and every one has failed. Officials who should protect are roaring lions. Judges are “evening wolves”, ravenous at dusk and leaving nothing by morning. Prophets are fickle and treacherous, saying whatever suits their hearers. Priests handle holy things carelessly and “do violence to the law”, twisting God’s word to get their way. Micah had said the same of the same city (Micah 3:9–11), and Ezekiel took up this very list (Ezekiel 22:25–28).

The LORD within her is righteous. Then this quiet, beautiful verse. While the judges devour and the priests twist, God has not left the city; he is in the middle of it, doing right: “every morning he shows forth his justice; each dawn he does not fail”, like the sunrise. Lamentations says it of his mercies: “they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23).

But the unjust knows no shame. The last line is the tragedy. God’s daily faithfulness changes nothing in them. It is possible to live in a city where God is visibly good and to feel nothing at all.

The righteous one in the city. Every leader in verses 3–4 failed. One day the Righteous One walked the same streets, the true King, Prophet and Priest; he did all they had failed to do, and they handed him over to suffer outside the gate for his people’s sins (Hebrews 13:12).

In everyday life. Ask the four questions of verse 2 of yourself, especially the last: do I draw near to God, or only stand near the things of God?

verseByVerse.quote: "I have cut off nations; their battlements are in ruins; I have laid waste their streets so that no one walks in them; their cities have been made desolate, without a man, without an inhabitant. I said, 'Surely you will fear me; you will accept correction. Then your dwelling would not be cut off according to all that I have appointed against you.' But all the more they were eager to make all their deeds corrupt. "Therefore wait for me," declares the LORD, "for the day when I rise up to seize the prey. For my decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation, all my burning anger; for in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judged other nations to warn his people, and they only grew worse; so the faithful are told to wait for the day when God himself rises to judge.

I have cut off nations. God points to the ruins on the horizon: broken battlements, empty streets, cities left “without a man, without an inhabitant”. Those ruins were meant to be read; Judah had even watched her sister kingdom Israel fall, and not taken the lesson (Jeremiah 3:6–10).

Surely you will fear me. Here is the sorrow of God, expressed as a thwarted hope. He judged other nations partly so that his own people could learn without suffering the same.

All the more they were eager. They drew the opposite conclusion. The Hebrew says they “rose early” to corrupt their deeds: the same dawn at which God shows forth his justice (v. 5) found his people up early for wrongdoing. Warnings that do not soften us harden us, a sober thought beside the daily news. Jesus said of a tower that fell and killed eighteen people: “unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:4–5).

Therefore wait for me. This is the hinge of the chapter, and the command is startling: God tells the faithful to wait for the very day of wrath announced in chapter 1. For those who belong to him it is not a threat to dread but a rescue to expect. The verse ends with the fire of 1:18, yet the next word is “For”: what comes through the fire is a purified people (v. 9).

The turning point. Everything up to here has been the problem; everything after it is what God will do. The switch comes not because the people improve but because God rises up. That is the shape of the gospel, and Christians still wait “for his Son from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

Uncertain wording. Where the ESV has “your dwelling” in verse 7, its note says the Hebrew reads “her”: God speaks of Jerusalem and to her in the same breath. The sense is unaffected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — A Pure Speech and a Humble Remnant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Beyond the judgment God will make a new people: drawn from every nation, cleansed in speech and humble in heart. He will purify the lips of the peoples so that all of them call on his name and serve him together, undoing the scattering of Babel, and worshippers will bring offerings even from beyond the rivers of Cush (vv. 9–10). In Jerusalem he will remove the shame of past rebellion and the proud who boasted on his holy mountain (v. 11). What remains is a humble and lowly people who take refuge in his name, who do no wrong and tell no lies, and who graze and lie down like a flock that no one can frighten (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to a proud, lying city is a purified people from every nation who take refuge in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: "For at that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call upon the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord. From beyond the rivers of Cush my worshipers, the daughter of my dispersed ones, shall bring my offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beyond the judgment God will cleanse the lips of the nations, so that people from every land call on his name and worship him together.

A pure speech. God’s first act in the new world is to change the way people talk, in a chapter that began with lying prophets and law-twisting priests. The word for speech is literally “lip”, the word used at Babel, where all the earth had “one language” (literally “one lip”) and God confused it because of human pride (Genesis 11:1–9). This looks like Babel undone.

What does pure speech mean? Mouths cleansed of the names of false gods (compare Hosea 2:17) and made fit to call on the LORD: it is about worship, not a new world language. Paul takes up the words for the gospel: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). “With one accord” is literally “with one shoulder”, like a team pulling together under one yoke.

From beyond the rivers of Cush. Worshippers will come from the furthest place Zephaniah’s hearers could imagine. In chapter 2 the Cushites fell under God’s sword (2:12); now Cushites bring him offerings. God’s judgments are never the end of his dealings with a people.

The first fruits. The New Testament does not quote this verse, but many Christians have seen its first fruits at Pentecost, when “each one was hearing them speak in his own language” (Acts 2:6). Soon afterwards an official of the queen of the Ethiopians, from this very region, believed in Jesus and “went on his way rejoicing” (Acts 8:27–39). Revelation shows a countless crowd from every nation praising God with one voice (Revelation 7:9–10).

Uncertain wording. “The daughter of my dispersed ones” is an obscure phrase. It may mean scattered Israelites coming home, or Gentile worshippers whom God now calls his own; some take it as a place name. Either way, worship comes from the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Cush lay south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan.

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day you shall not be put to shame because of the deeds by which you have rebelled against me; for then I will remove from your midst your proudly exultant ones, and you shall no longer be haughty in my holy mountain. But I will leave in your midst a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the LORD, those who are left in Israel; they shall do no injustice and speak no lies, nor shall there be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue. For they shall graze and lie down, and none shall make them afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will take away the shame of his people’s sins and the pride that spoiled them, and leave a humble, honest people who shelter in his name and live unafraid.

You shall not be put to shame. First, no shame: “you shall not be put to shame because of the deeds by which you have rebelled against me”. The sins are real, but they will no longer hang over his people’s heads.

Your proudly exultant ones. Second, God will remove the proud. Pride among God’s people is no small fault, and it was most at home “in my holy mountain”, where religious people feel safest.

A people humble and lowly. Here is the people God is making: not the strong or impressive, but those chapter 2 called “all you humble of the land” (2:3). They “seek refuge in the name of the LORD”, running into who he has shown himself to be: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10).

They shall do no injustice and speak no lies. Their character has changed. The corrupt speech of verse 4 has been healed, and they have become like their God, who “does no injustice” (v. 5, the same words). Then the picture of a flock: they “graze and lie down, and none shall make them afraid”. A sheep only lies down when it feels safe.

Jesus and the lowly. Jesus began his great sermon with these people (Matthew 5:3), and described himself in the same words: “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He alone fully kept verse 13: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). And the shame of his people’s rebellion is lifted because he carried it, enduring the cross, “despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). The King is like his people, or rather they are being made like him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The LORD Your God Is in Your Midst
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book that began with God sweeping the earth bare ends with God singing over the people he has saved. Zion is called to sing and shout with all her heart (v. 14), because the judgments against her are taken away, her enemies cleared, and the King, the LORD, is in her midst (v. 15). Fear can go and weary hands can work again, for the mighty one who saves rejoices over his people, quiets them by his love and exults over them with loud singing (vv. 16–17). He will gather the grieving, deal with the oppressors, rescue the lame and the outcast, turn their shame into praise, and bring them home before their eyes (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The book that began with sweeping away ends with God singing over the people he has saved.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter of Jerusalem! The LORD has taken away the judgments against you; he has cleared away your enemies. The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst; you shall never again fear evil. On that day it shall be said to Jerusalem: "Fear not, O Zion; let not your hands grow weak. The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has taken away his people’s judgment and lives among them as their King, they are to sing, and, astonishingly, he sings over them. Verse 17 is the summit of the book.

Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion. Four commands, all about joy, to the city called rebellious and defiled a few verses ago. God does not merely forgive her; he tells her to celebrate.

The LORD has taken away the judgments against you. Three reasons for the singing. The judgments against her are taken away: the case is closed. Her enemies are cleared away. And best of all, “The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst”. The problem of the book was a city where God was present but ignored (v. 5); now he is welcomed, and “you shall never again fear evil”.

Let not your hands grow weak. “Fear not”, and then a practical word for discouraged people. Fear makes the hands drop. When you know God is with you, you can pick the work back up.

A mighty one who will save. “Mighty one” is a word used of warriors: his presence among his people is not merely comforting but strong to rescue.

He will rejoice over you with gladness. Most of us can believe that God tolerates us, or forgives us, or is patient with us. That God is glad about us is harder to take in. Yet that is what it says. Isaiah says the same: “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5).

He will quiet you by his love. A picture of a parent with an anxious child: the arms go round, and the crying stops. God’s love does not merely inform his people; it settles them (see the box below).

He will exult over you with loud singing. God sings. The Bible tells his people to sing hundreds of times; here God himself sings, and the song is about them.

The King in the midst. “The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst” came true when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). When he rode into Jerusalem, John’s Gospel greeted him with words that seem to join Zechariah 9:9 to this passage: “Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming” (John 12:15). Jesus spoke of joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7), and endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2). The joy was his people.

Judgment and song. Hold verse 17 next to 1:2, where God said he would sweep everything away. The road from one to the other runs through the cross, where that judgment fell on Christ instead.

Who is your audience? Every one of us performs for someone. More than a century ago the sociologist Charles Horton Cooley described the looking-glass self: we see ourselves largely as we imagine others see us. Social media has turned that mirror into a scoreboard, and it is exhausting, because the audience is fickle. Religion often just changes the audience: now God is watching, arms folded, and we try harder. Zephaniah sweeps both away. The one audience whose verdict finally matters is not frowning, nor merely tolerant. He is singing over his people, not because they performed well (this was “the oppressing city”) but because he has taken away the judgments against them. When you know the King is glad over you in Christ, the other audiences shrink to their proper size, and you are free to love them instead of needing them.

What if I cannot feel it? On a dark day you may feel nothing of God’s gladness, and it is still true, because it rests on what he has done, not on your mood. If the darkness lingers, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too, for low mood can have causes in the body.

Uncertain wording. “He will quiet you by his love” is hard to pin down; the ESV notes it may mean “he will be quiet in his love”, a love too full for words, close to the KJV’s “he will rest in his love”; the Greek Old Testament reads “he will renew you”. None of these weakens the verse: God’s love for his people is settled, deep and at rest.

verseByVerse.quote: I will gather those of you who mourn for the festival, so that you will no longer suffer reproach. Behold, at that time I will deal with all your oppressors. And I will save the lame and gather the outcast, and I will change their shame into praise and renown in all the earth. At that time I will bring you in, at the time when I gather you together; for I will make you renowned and praised among all the peoples of the earth, when I restore your fortunes before your eyes," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will gather the grieving, the lame and the outcast, deal with all who oppressed them, turn their shame into praise and bring them home.

Those of you who mourn for the festival. Those who grieve because they cannot keep the appointed feasts: exiles far from the temple, the sick, the excluded (see the box below). God’s first act is to gather them.

I will save the lame and gather the outcast. Three groups, and God has a word for each. The oppressors he will deal with. The lame, who cannot keep up, he will save. The outcast, pushed out of the community, he will gather. Micah made the same promise: “I will assemble the lame and gather those who have been driven away” (Micah 4:6).

I will change their shame into praise. What they were ashamed of becomes the reason people praise God, as it does in every redeemed life.

At that time I will bring you in. The book ends with a homecoming, and the restoration happens “before your eyes”, so that God’s people actually see it. Think of the distance travelled: the book began with God sweeping the earth bare and ends with him gathering the lame and bringing them home, and the humble who sought him in 2:3 are the ones he sings over here.

The Shepherd who gathers. Jesus went after the lame and the outcast, and told of a master who sent his servant to “bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (Luke 14:21). He died, John says, “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52).

Where Christians differ: how is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists, who keep God’s promises to Israel distinct from those to the church, look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. Those who hold this hope hold it from the same Bible. This commentary’s view: the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, as many read Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. The New Testament itself applies Israel’s gathering to his one flock (John 11:52) and widens the promised land to the whole world (Romans 4:13).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew of verse 18 is uncertain, and translations differ widely. The sense, that God will gather the grieving and end their disgrace, is plain.

3.title: He Will Rejoice Over You
3.overview:
Where we are. Judgment has swept round the nations to Nineveh (2:4–15); now Zephaniah turns back to Jerusalem, and the book reaches its lowest point and its highest. The city God chose is called “the oppressing city”; by the end of the chapter she is the daughter of Zion over whom God sings.

The message. God’s own city is as guilty as Nineveh, yet the LORD has not left her: every morning he does justice in her midst. Because his people would not learn, he will judge; then he will do what they never could: purify a people from every nation, leave a humble remnant who take refuge in his name, take away the judgments against them, and live among them as their King, rejoicing over them with singing.

Why it was said. Zephaniah’s hearers had watched other nations fall and learned nothing (vv. 6–7), and their leaders were corrupt (see the introduction). The humble who heeded 2:3 needed to know whether their seeking had a future: they are told to wait for God, and shown what he will do.

How the chapter makes its case. First the charge: Jerusalem will not listen or draw near, and every class of leader has failed, while the righteous LORD within her does justice each dawn (vv. 1–5). Warnings only hardened her, so the faithful are told, “wait for me” (vv. 6–8). Then everything turns. God will purify the speech of the peoples so that they call on his name, with worshippers from beyond Cush (vv. 9–10), and leave a humble, honest people who shelter in his name (vv. 11–13). Finally Zion is told to sing, for the judgments are gone and the King is in her midst, a mighty saviour who rejoices over her (vv. 14–17), gathers the lame and the outcast, and brings his scattered people home (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. By promise, more directly here than anywhere else in the book. “The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst” (v. 15) came true when the Word became flesh, and when Jesus rode into Jerusalem the Gospel greeted him with “Fear not, daughter of Zion” (John 12:15). The judgments were taken away at the cross; the purified speech of the nations began at Pentecost; and the humble people of verse 12 are shaped like their King, “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The God who sings over his people is the God whose Son endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2).

For us. Many Christians believe that God forgives them, or puts up with them, but not that he is glad over them. This chapter says that in Christ he is. That frees us from performing for him or anyone else, and calls us to be the humble, honest, unafraid people of verses 12–13, who shelter in his name and sing back.
3.theology:
God's own city can be as guilty as any pagan capital, and its decline shows in deafness, defensiveness, distrust and distance (vv. 1-2).

When leaders in every office fail, God himself remains righteous in the midst of them, faithful as the sunrise (vv. 3-5; Lam 3:22-23).

Warnings that do not soften us harden us (vv. 6-7).

For God's people, the day of judgment is not a threat to dread but a day to wait for (v. 8).

God purifies the speech of the nations so that they call on his name together, undoing Babel, a promise many Christians see beginning at Pentecost (v. 9; Gen 11:7; Acts 2:4-11; Rev 7:9).

The people God keeps are humble and lowly, sheltering in his name and made truthful (vv. 12-13; Matt 5:3; 11:29).

God is not merely present but present to save, and his love quiets his people and breaks into singing over them (vv. 15-17; Isa 62:5; Matt 1:23; Luke 15:7; Heb 12:2).

God gathers the lame and the outcast and turns their shame into praise (vv. 19-20; Mic 4:6-7).
3.examples:
The chapter begins with a woe aimed at Jerusalem as if she were Nineveh, judges like wolves that leave nothing by morning, and ruined cities on the horizon that nobody reads as a warning. Yet in the middle of it God is doing right, every single dawn, and he tells the faithful to wait for the day everyone else dreads.

Then Babel's confusion is undone by purified lips that call on his name, a parent's arms go round a frightened child until the crying stops, and God himself sings, and the song is about his people.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the book and one of the most astonishing verses in the Bible. The God who searched Jerusalem with lamps is present among his people as a mighty saviour, and he is glad over them, quieting them by his love and singing over them. In Christ, who bore the judgment that makes it possible, it is spoken to every believer.

3.reflection:
Verse 2 lists four failures: not listening, not accepting correction, not trusting, not drawing near. Which do you recognise as an early sign of drifting in your own life, and what helps you turn back?

God judged other nations so that his people would learn, but they grew worse (vv. 6–7). How should Christians respond to the disasters they see in the news? What would it look like to learn from them rather than harden?

Verses 9–13 describe a people from every nation, cleansed in speech, humble, honest and unafraid. How far does your church look like this, and what would need to change?

Verse 17 says that God rejoices over his people with gladness and sings over them. Do you find this easy or hard to believe about yourself? How does the cross make it true, and how would believing it change the way you live before God and others?
